quests.instruction: You wait at a “bus shelter” and say it quickly. What often happens to the /s/ at the end of “bus”?
options: It often shifts towards /ʃ/, because the tongue is already moving back for “shelter”
It stays a sharp /s/ and is followed by a clear pause before “shelter” begins
It becomes /z/, because the next sound begins a stressed syllable and voicing spreads backwards
quests.correctAnswer: It often shifts towards /ʃ/, because the tongue is already moving back for “shelter”
quests.hint: Say “bus” and “shelter” together. Notice where your tongue is at the end of “bus” compared with the start of “shelter”.
quests.explanation: /s/ and /ʃ/ are both hissing sounds, but /ʃ/ is made with the tongue slightly further back. In quick speech the tongue moves towards the /ʃ/ position early, so “bus shelter” often sounds like “bush shelter”, with one long /ʃ/. The words are unchanged; the /s/ has taken on the place of the sound that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: An alveolar /s/ before /ʃ/ is often realised as [ʃ], a place assimilation, and the two can merge into one lengthened /ʃ/.

quests.instruction: Why does “nice shoes” often sound as if the /s/ has become “sh”?
options: The /s/ is replaced by /ʃ/ because “shoes” is spelled with “sh”
The /s/ becomes /z/ because “shoes” ends in a voiced sound
The tongue moves back early for /ʃ/, so the /s/ shifts to [ʃ]
quests.correctAnswer: The tongue moves back early for /ʃ/, so the /s/ shifts to [ʃ]
quests.hint: Think about which sound is made further back in the mouth, /s/ or /ʃ/, and which one is coming next.
quests.explanation: The /ʃ/ at the start of “shoes” is the trigger. Because the tongue is already moving back for it, the /s/ at the end of “nice” shifts to [ʃ]: “nysh shoes”. The spelling does not cause the change; the following sound does.
quests.phoneticRule: The trigger of the change is the following sound's place of articulation, not the spelling of the word; /ʃ/ pulls a preceding /s/ backwards.

quests.instruction: You hear a news report about a “gas shortage”. Which version shows the change?
options: /ɡæz ˈʃɔːtɪdʒ/, with the /s/ voiced into /z/
/ɡæʃ ˈʃɔːtɪdʒ/, with the /s/ shifting to /ʃ/
/ɡæs ˈʃɔːtɪdʒ/, with a clear sharp /s/ and a short pause
quests.correctAnswer: /ɡæʃ ˈʃɔːtɪdʒ/, with the /s/ shifting to /ʃ/
quests.hint: The second word begins with “sh”. Decide what that does to the last sound of “gas”.
quests.explanation: “Shortage” begins with /ʃ/, so the /s/ at the end of “gas” often shifts to [ʃ]: /ɡæʃ ˈʃɔːtɪdʒ/. The same pattern you heard in “bus shelter” appears here, which shows that it depends on the sounds, not on the particular words.
quests.phoneticRule: The /s/ + /ʃ/ pattern is general: any word-final /s/ before a word beginning with /ʃ/ can assimilate in casual speech.

quests.instruction: You ask, “Is she coming?” Which version of “is she” shows the change often heard in casual speech?
options: /ɪz ʃi/, with a clear voiced /z/
/ɪs ʃi/, with the /z/ simply turning into /s/
/ɪʒ ʃi/, with the /z/ shifting towards /ʒ/
quests.correctAnswer: /ɪʒ ʃi/, with the /z/ shifting towards /ʒ/
quests.hint: Say “is” and “she” together. Notice how far back your tongue moves for “sh”, and what the /z/ does beforehand.
quests.explanation: /z/ is made with the tongue tip near the ridge behind the upper teeth, while /ʃ/ is made further back. In quick speech the /z/ often moves back too, becoming [ʒ] (or sometimes [ʃ]): /ɪʒ ʃi/. The voicing of the /z/ can carry over at first.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /z/ before /ʃ/ is often realised as [ʒ] or [ʃ], taking on the postalveolar place of the following consonant.

quests.instruction: In “does she”, which sound does the /z/ move towards in fast speech?
options: /ʒ/ or /ʃ/, made further back in the mouth to match the /ʃ/ of “she”
/s/ only, because the /ʃ/ of “she” is voiceless and so devoices the /z/
/dʒ/, because the two sounds blend into one affricate before “she”
quests.correctAnswer: /ʒ/ or /ʃ/, made further back in the mouth to match the /ʃ/ of “she”
quests.hint: Compare where /z/ and /ʃ/ are made, and decide which direction the change runs.
quests.explanation: The /z/ moves backwards towards the place of the /ʃ/: [ʒ], or [ʃ] if it also loses voicing. Changing to /s/ would be a voicing change without a place change, which is not the main effect here; and an affricate /dʒ/ belongs to a different pattern you will meet later. So the key idea is the shift in place.
quests.phoneticRule: The pull is towards the place of the following consonant; voicing may also shift, but the defining change is the move from alveolar to postalveolar.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “as she said”. Which version fits a quick spoken line?
options: /əʒ ʃi sed/, with the /z/ shifting towards /ʒ/
/əz ʃi sed/, with a fully alveolar /z/ kept clear
/ədʒ ʃi sed/, with a /dʒ/ sound inserted
quests.correctAnswer: /əʒ ʃi sed/, with the /z/ shifting towards /ʒ/
quests.hint: The /z/ of “as” meets the “sh” of “she”. Ask which one gives way.
quests.explanation: “As” ends in /z/ and “she” begins with /ʃ/, so the /z/ shifts backwards: /əʒ ʃi sed/. The same pattern appears in “is she” and “does she”, which shows how predictable it is for words ending in /z/.
quests.phoneticRule: Because the pattern depends on the sounds, it applies to any word ending in /z/ before /ʃ/, including weak function words such as “as” and “is”.

quests.instruction: Predict what happens to the /v/ of “have” in “You have to go.”
options: It stays a fully voiced /v/ and is released clearly before the /t/ begins
It often loses its voicing and sounds like /f/, because the /t/ is voiceless
It changes to /b/, because the next sound is a stop and stops are lip sounds
quests.correctAnswer: It often loses its voicing and sounds like /f/, because the /t/ is voiceless
quests.hint: Put a finger on your throat, say “have”, then “have to”. Notice whether the buzzing carries on into the /t/.
quests.explanation: /v/ is voiced (your vocal folds vibrate) and /t/ is voiceless. In fast speech the voicing often stops early, so the /v/ sounds like /f/: “haf to”, which is why some people write “hafta”. This is voicing assimilation: the earlier sound copies the voicing of the later one.
quests.phoneticRule: Voicing assimilation: a word-final voiced consonant may lose voicing before a voiceless consonant, so /v/ in “have” is often realised as [f] before /t/.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits “of course” sounding as if it has an /f/.
options: The letter “v” is silent in fast speech
The /k/ becomes voiced, which pulls the /v/ along with it
The voiced /v/ loses its voicing before the voiceless /k/
quests.correctAnswer: The voiced /v/ loses its voicing before the voiceless /k/
quests.hint: Think about the direction: which sound is the trigger, and is it voiced or voiceless?
quests.explanation: The /k/ is voiceless, so the voicing of the /v/ before it often fades: /əf kɔːs/. The /k/ stays as it is. The letter “v” is not silent; it is the sound that has lost its voicing, which is why the result is closer to /f/.
quests.phoneticRule: In voicing assimilation the trigger is the following sound: a voiceless consonant can devoice a preceding voiced one.

quests.instruction: Apply the voicing change to “five past” in “It’s five past six.” Which version fits?
options: /faɪv pɑːst/, with a fully voiced /v/ held through to the /p/
/faɪb pɑːst/, with the /v/ changing into a /b/
/faɪf pɑːst/, with the /v/ losing its voicing before the /p/
quests.correctAnswer: /faɪf pɑːst/, with the /v/ losing its voicing before the /p/
quests.hint: The next sound, /p/, is voiceless. Decide what that does to the buzz at the end of “five”.
quests.explanation: /p/ is voiceless, so the /v/ of “five” often loses its voicing and sounds like /f/: /faɪf pɑːst/. The same logic as “have to” and “of course” applies, with a different trigger sound. Time expressions make this easy to hear.
quests.phoneticRule: Any voiceless trigger (/p/, /t/, /k/, /s/) can devoice a preceding word-final voiced fricative such as /v/ or /z/.

quests.instruction: You describe an old habit: “I used to live in Leeds.” Which spoken form of “used to” fits?
options: /juːs tə/, with the ending reduced to a voiceless /s/ before the /t/
/juːzd tə/, with a clear voiced /z/ and a fully separate /d/ before the /t/
/juːz tə/, with a voiced /z/ kept in full before the /t/
quests.correctAnswer: /juːs tə/, with the ending reduced to a voiceless /s/ before the /t/
quests.hint: Compare “I used a pen” with “I used to write”. The spelling is the same, but listen to the ending of “used”.
quests.explanation: In the habitual “used to”, the written “d” merges with the /t/ of “to”, and the /z/ before them loses its voicing, so the phrase sounds like “use-ta”: /juːs tə/. Compare “I used the phone”, where “used” keeps its /zd/ ending.
quests.phoneticRule: In “used to” (habit), /zd/ is reduced to a voiceless /s/ with the /d/ merging into the following /t/, giving /juːs tə/.

quests.instruction: You are reminded of a rule: “You’re supposed to sign in.” Choose the spoken form of “supposed to”.
options: /səˈpəʊzd tuː/, with every sound clearly pronounced, including the full /d/
/səˈpəʊs tə/, with the final /zd/ reduced to a voiceless /s/ before /t/
/səˈpəʊz tə/, with a voiced /z/ kept in full before the /t/
quests.correctAnswer: /səˈpəʊs tə/, with the final /zd/ reduced to a voiceless /s/ before /t/
quests.hint: Say “supposed” on its own, then “supposed to” at normal speed. Notice what happens at the end of the first word.
quests.explanation: As with “used to”, the ending of “supposed” loses its voicing before the /t/ of “to”, and the /d/ merges with the /t/: /səˈpəʊs tə/. It is an extremely common spoken form in rules and instructions, which is why it helps to recognise it.
quests.phoneticRule: Verb endings in /zd/ frequently devoice and merge with the /t/ of “to” in fixed phrases such as “supposed to” and “used to”.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “has to” fits “She has to leave early”?
options: /hæs tə/, with the /z/ losing its voicing before /t/
/hæz tə/, with a full voiced /z/ kept before the /t/
/hæʃ tə/, with the /z/ moving further back in the mouth
quests.correctAnswer: /hæs tə/, with the /z/ losing its voicing before /t/
quests.hint: Say “has” and “has to” and compare the buzz at the end of the first word.
quests.explanation: /z/ is voiced and /t/ is voiceless, so in fast speech the /z/ often loses voicing before /t/ and sounds like /s/: /hæs tə/. It follows the same logic as “have to”, where /v/ becomes [f].
quests.phoneticRule: The voicing of a word-final fricative can adapt to a following voiceless stop: /z/ often becomes [s], and /v/ often becomes [f].

quests.instruction: Inside a word the same pattern can occur. Which version of “uncomfortable” shows the change in casual speech?
options: /ʌn ˈkʌmftəbl/, with a clear tongue-tip /n/ kept before the /k/
/ʌm ˈkʌmftəbl/, with the nasal made at the lips, as before /p/
/ʌŋ ˈkʌmftəbl/, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.correctAnswer: /ʌŋ ˈkʌmftəbl/, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: Look at the sound that follows the “un” part. Which place in the mouth does it use?
quests.explanation: The prefix “un-” ends in /n/, and the next sound, /k/, is made at the back of the mouth. In casual speech the /n/ often shifts to [ŋ]: /ʌŋ ˈkʌmftəbl/. The pattern is regular enough that some English spellings show it, such as “impossible” and “immature”.
quests.phoneticRule: Place assimilation also operates across prefix and word boundaries, so a prefix-final /n/ may take the place of the following consonant.

quests.instruction: Which sound changes inside “input” in casual speech, as in “I need some input”?
options: The /p/ changes into /n/ before the /t/
The /n/ changes into /m/ before the /p/
The /t/ changes into /p/ at the end of the word
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ changes into /m/ before the /p/
quests.hint: Split the word into “in” and “put”, and look at how the first part meets the second.
quests.explanation: “Input” is built from “in” and “put”. The /n/ of “in” often shifts to [m] before the lip sound /p/: /ˈɪmpʊt/. The other sounds stay as they are. So a word that looks like one unit can still show a change at its internal boundary.
quests.phoneticRule: Compound words show the same assimilation at their internal boundaries as phrases show between words.

quests.instruction: Apply the same change to “income tax”. Which version fits?
options: /ˈɪmkʌm tæks/, with the nasal made at the lips, as before /p/
/ˈɪŋkʌm tæks/, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
/ˈɪnkʌm tæks/, with a clear tongue-tip /n/ kept throughout
quests.correctAnswer: /ˈɪŋkʌm tæks/, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: The word “income” is “in” plus “come”. Check the first sound of “come” and match the nasal to it.
quests.explanation: “Come” begins with /k/, made at the back of the mouth, so the /n/ of “in” often shifts to [ŋ]: /ˈɪŋkʌm/. The second word, “tax”, plays no part in this change. It is the same pattern as “phone call” and “uncomfortable”.
quests.phoneticRule: The prefix “in-” behaves like the preposition “in”: before /k/ or /g/ its /n/ is commonly realised as [ŋ].

quests.instruction: Two listeners hear “red carpet” as “reg carpet”. One calls it a careless slur; the other says it follows a pattern. Who is right?
options: The second: the /d/ moves back to match the /k/, which is a predictable place change
The first: any change to the /d/ shows that the speaker is being careless, lazy or unclear
Neither: the /d/ has simply been deleted, so nothing has changed in place
quests.correctAnswer: The second: the /d/ moves back to match the /k/, which is a predictable place change
quests.hint: Ask whether the new sound shares a place in the mouth with the sound that follows.
quests.explanation: A real assimilation is systematic: the changed /d/ now matches the place of the /k/ that follows. A careless slur would change the sound in unpredictable ways. Because “reg carpet” follows a clear rule, it is an ordinary casual variant. Listening for the match helps you tell the two apart.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation can be recognised by its regularity: the changed consonant shares a place of articulation with the following consonant, whereas unsystematic changes do not.

quests.instruction: You hear “right place” as something like “ripe place”. Which clue shows this is assimilation rather than a random slip?
options: The word “right” became shorter, so the speaker must be hurrying
The vowel of “right” changed because the /p/ that follows is louder than the /t/
The changed /t/ now shares its place, the lips, with the /p/ that follows
quests.correctAnswer: The changed /t/ now shares its place, the lips, with the /p/ that follows
quests.hint: Ask where the new consonant is made, and whether the next sound uses the same place.
quests.explanation: The /t/ has moved to the lips, exactly where the following /p/ is made. That match is the signature of assimilation. The vowel and the rest of the word are unchanged. Knowing this lets you recognise “right place” even when it briefly resembles a word like “ripe”.
quests.phoneticRule: A reliable diagnostic for assimilation is place matching: the changed sound and the trigger sound share the same place of articulation.

quests.instruction: Which version of “clean copy” shows predictable assimilation rather than a random slip?
options: /kliːŋ ˈkɒpi/, with the nasal made at the back, like the /k/
/kliːm ˈkɒpi/, with the nasal made at the lips, like a /p/
/kliːt ˈkɒpi/, with the /n/ turning into a /t/ before the /k/
quests.correctAnswer: /kliːŋ ˈkɒpi/, with the nasal made at the back, like the /k/
quests.hint: The changed sound should share a place with the /k/ that follows. Which option does that?
quests.explanation: Only the version with [ŋ] matches the back-of-mouth place of /k/. A lip sound or a /t/ would not be predicted by the rule, so it would be an unsystematic change rather than assimilation. Checking for this match is a quick way to test any suspected case.
quests.phoneticRule: Predictable assimilation moves the word-final alveolar to exactly the place of the trigger; a change to a different place is not explained by the pattern.

quests.instruction: Which two processes can be heard in “hot milk and honey”?
options: Linking at “hot milk” and assimilation at “milk and”
Assimilation at “hot milk” and linking at “milk and”
Assimilation at both “hot milk” and “milk and”
quests.correctAnswer: Assimilation at “hot milk” and linking at “milk and”
quests.hint: Check each boundary: does a consonant change its place, or does it simply move onto a vowel?
quests.explanation: At “hot milk”, the /t/ can shift to [p] before /m/, which is assimilation. At “milk and”, the /k/ simply moves onto the vowel of “and” without changing, which is linking. So one short phrase can show both, and each has a different cause.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation and linking are triggered by different following sounds: a consonant of another place for assimilation, a vowel for linking.

quests.instruction: In “run back out”, one boundary shows assimilation and one shows linking. Which pair is correct?
options: Linking at “run back”, and assimilation at “back out”
Assimilation at “back out”, and no change at “run back”
Assimilation at “run back”, and linking at “back out”
quests.correctAnswer: Assimilation at “run back”, and linking at “back out”
quests.hint: One boundary ends in a consonant before another consonant; the other ends in a consonant before a vowel.
quests.explanation: At “run back”, the /n/ can shift to [m] before /b/: assimilation. At “back out”, the /k/ moves onto “out”: linking. The same word “back” is both a trigger and a linking word, which is a good reminder that each boundary is judged on its own.
quests.phoneticRule: A word can be the trigger for assimilation at its left boundary and the source of linking at its right boundary.

quests.instruction: Choose the spoken form of “phone Matt about it” that shows both a place change and links.
options: “fohn Matt about it”, with every consonant kept clearly apart from the next word
“fohm Ma-ta-bou-tit”, with /n/ shifting to /m/ and the /t/ sounds linking
“fohm Matt about it”, with only the place change and no links at all
quests.correctAnswer: “fohm Ma-ta-bou-tit”, with /n/ shifting to /m/ and the /t/ sounds linking
quests.hint: Mark one boundary with a consonant before a consonant, and two with a consonant before a vowel.
quests.explanation: The /n/ of “phone” can shift to [m] before the /m/ of “Matt”, and the /t/ of “Matt” and the /t/ of “about” each link to the next vowel: “fohm Ma-ta-bou-tit”. Four words can therefore contain one assimilation and two links.
quests.phoneticRule: In a longer chunk, each boundary is resolved independently, so assimilation and several links can occur side by side.

quests.instruction: You see “main course” on a menu. Before hearing it, predict how a fast speaker may say “main”.
options: “mayng”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
“mame”, with the nasal made at the lips, as before a /p/ or /b/
“mane”, with the tongue-tip /n/ pressed clearly against the ridge
quests.correctAnswer: “mayng”, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: Write down the first sound of “course” and note where in the mouth it is made. Then match the nasal to it.
quests.explanation: /k/ is made at the back of the mouth, so the /n/ before it often shifts to [ŋ]: “mayng course”. The prediction rule is simple: find the place of the next consonant, then match the final alveolar to it.
quests.phoneticRule: To predict place assimilation, identify the place of the following consonant (bilabial or velar) and expect a word-final alveolar to shift towards it in casual speech.

quests.instruction: Predict what happens to the /t/ in “tight budget”.
options: It can move to the lips, ending up close to a /p/
It can move to the back of the mouth, ending up close to a /k/
It gets an extra strong puff of air before the /b/
quests.correctAnswer: It can move to the lips, ending up close to a /p/
quests.hint: Note the first sound of “budget” and the place in the mouth where it is made, then predict the /t/.
quests.explanation: /b/ is a lip sound, so the /t/ of “tight” can shift to the lips, sounding close to [p]: /taɪp ˈbʌdʒɪt/. Predicting it from the trigger works even with a phrase you have not heard before. Work phrases such as this one are a good place to practise.
quests.phoneticRule: Prediction works for any trigger: bilabial /p b m/ pulls /t d n/ to the lips, and velar /k g/ pulls them to the back of the mouth.

quests.instruction: Predict how “hard month” may sound in casual speech.
options: /hɑːɡ mʌnθ/, with the /d/ made at the back of the mouth
/hɑːt mʌnθ/, with the /d/ devoiced into a /t/
/hɑːb mʌnθ/, with the /d/ made at the lips
quests.correctAnswer: /hɑːb mʌnθ/, with the /d/ made at the lips
quests.hint: The next word starts with /m/. Predict which place the /d/ will move to before you check the options.
quests.explanation: /m/ is made at the lips, so the /d/ of “hard” can move to the lips: /hɑːb mʌnθ/. If you predicted this before reading the options, you are using the rule rather than memory, which is the goal of this level.
quests.phoneticRule: Regular assimilation can be predicted from the trigger's place: lips for /m/, /p/ and /b/; the back of the mouth for /k/ and /g/.

quests.instruction: On a work call you hear, “They need more time.” Which spoken form of “need more” is typical of casual speech?
options: /niːd mɔː/, with a clear tongue-tip /d/
/niːɡ mɔː/, with the /d/ made at the back of the mouth
/niːb mɔː/, with the /d/ made at the lips
quests.correctAnswer: /niːb mɔː/, with the /d/ made at the lips
quests.hint: Think about who is speaking: a colleague on a call, relaxed and quick. The /d/ meets an /m/.
quests.explanation: /m/ is made with the lips, so the /d/ of “need” often shifts to the lips in relaxed speech: /niːb mɔː/. A careful speaker may keep a clear /d/, especially in a formal meeting. Both are normal, and recognising the lip version helps you follow fast calls.
quests.phoneticRule: In relaxed workplace speech, the alveolar-to-bilabial shift often occurs at word boundaries before /m/, while a formal register may keep the citation form.

quests.instruction: A cashier asks, “Do you pay in cash?” Which version of “in cash” shows the assimilation often heard at a till?
options: /ɪm kæʃ/, with the nasal made at the lips, as before /b/
/ɪŋ kæʃ/, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
/ɪn kæʃ/, with a clear tongue-tip /n/ kept before the /k/
quests.correctAnswer: /ɪŋ kæʃ/, with the nasal made at the back of the mouth
quests.hint: Look at the first sound of “cash” and match the nasal to its place in the mouth.
quests.explanation: “Cash” begins with /k/, so the /n/ of “in” often shifts to [ŋ]: /ɪŋ kæʃ/. A clear /n/ is also normal, especially in careful speech. But recognising the [ŋ] version helps you catch this very common question at a counter.
quests.phoneticRule: Short function words such as “in” assimilate like any other word ending in an alveolar nasal when a velar consonant follows.

quests.instruction: In “It would be cheaper”, which sound is changed by the /b/ that follows?
options: The /d/ at the end of “would”
The /b/ at the start of “be”
The /tʃ/ at the start of “cheaper”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ at the end of “would”
quests.hint: Only the sound right before the trigger can change. Which sound sits at the edge of the word before /b/?
quests.explanation: The /d/ at the end of “would” sits right before /b/, so it can shift to the lips: /wʊb bi/. The /b/ itself is the trigger and stays as it is, and the sounds of “cheaper” are too far away to be affected. This is a common phrase in shops and on the phone when comparing prices.
quests.phoneticRule: In the chain trigger and target, only the word-final alveolar immediately before the trigger is affected, not the trigger itself or sounds further away.

quests.instruction: Which type of assimilation is heard in “love to” in “I’d love to come”?
options: Place assimilation: the /v/ moves to a different place in the mouth
Voicing assimilation: the /v/ loses its voicing before /t/
Linking: the /v/ joins the next word
quests.correctAnswer: Voicing assimilation: the /v/ loses its voicing before /t/
quests.hint: Ask what actually changes about the /v/: where it is made, or whether the vocal folds vibrate.
quests.explanation: The place of the /v/ stays the same; what changes is the voicing. Before the voiceless /t/ the buzz often fades, so /v/ sounds like /f/: /lʌf tə/. So this is voicing assimilation, not place assimilation and not linking, because no vowel follows.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation can affect place or voicing; identifying which property changes is the key to naming the type.

quests.instruction: Compare “dress shop” with “love to”. How do the two changes differ?
options: Both change their place of articulation, moving towards the place of the following sound in the mouth
“dress shop” changes place (/s/ towards /ʃ/); “love to” changes voicing (/v/ towards /f/)
Both change their voicing, losing the buzz because a voiceless sound follows each of them
quests.correctAnswer: “dress shop” changes place (/s/ towards /ʃ/); “love to” changes voicing (/v/ towards /f/)
quests.hint: For each phrase, decide whether the changed sound moved in the mouth or lost its buzz.
quests.explanation: In “dress shop”, the tongue moves back for /ʃ/, so the /s/ shifts place. In “love to”, the tongue and lips stay where they are, but the vocal folds stop vibrating early. Naming the property that changes lets you sort new examples quickly.
quests.phoneticRule: Place assimilation changes where a consonant is made; voicing assimilation changes whether the vocal folds vibrate; the two can be told apart by asking which property differs.

quests.instruction: Which list of changes matches “has to” and “join Ben” in “She has to join Ben”?
options: Place assimilation in both of the two boundaries
Voicing assimilation in both of the two boundaries
Voicing in “has to”, and place in “join Ben”
quests.correctAnswer: Voicing in “has to”, and place in “join Ben”
quests.hint: Decide which property changes at each boundary: the buzz of the /z/, or the position of the /n/.
quests.explanation: In “has to”, the /z/ can lose its voicing before /t/: /hæs tə/. In “join Ben”, the /n/ can shift to the lips before /b/: /dʒɔɪm ben/. So the same sentence can show a voicing change and a place change, and naming each one shows you understand the pattern.
quests.phoneticRule: A sentence can contain several assimilations of different types; each is identified by the property that changes and by its trigger sound.
